key_points.base: I'd start with the decision the model supports: who gets a retention offer, and what an offer costs
points: Start from the decision: who gets a retention offer, and what it costs versus a lost customer
Define churn and the prediction window explicitly
Build features only from data available at prediction time and split by time
Baseline with logistic regression before a complex model
Churn is imbalanced, so use precision and recall at an actionable top-k, not accuracy
Ship when the false-positive cost is acceptable, not when a metric crosses a number

key_points.base: I'd separate data drift (inputs shift, measured with PSI or KS on key features) from model drift (pe
points: Separate data drift (inputs shift) from model drift (performance drops)
Measure input drift with PSI or KS on key features
Labels arrive late, so input and prediction distributions are the early signal
Tie thresholds to impact with a rule for investigate, retrain or roll back
Alert on a few important features and an aggregate score to avoid alert fatigue

key_points.base: History only shows what happened under past budgets. I'd model the demand drivers (revenue plan, att
points: History only reflects past budgets, so model the demand drivers
Drivers include revenue plan, attrition, ramp time and open requisitions
Treat the approved budget as a constraint on supply
Compare a seasonal baseline, a driver regression and ARIMA with rolling-origin backtests
When the forecast conflicts with the budget, show the gap, assumptions and scenarios
Flag regime shifts like a hiring pause instead of learning from them

key_points.base: Every feature is computed as of a cutoff date using only data available then, via as-of joins or a p
points: Compute every feature as of a cutoff date with point-in-time joins
Verify by recomputing features at past cutoffs
Features like days since last payment leak if computed on the full table
Prune features by domain priors, stability over time and time-based importance
Keep missingness as a signal and impute inside a pipeline fit on training data
Check whether missingness correlates with the target

key_points.base: First rule out a pipeline bug: schema, null rates, feature computation, and train/serve skew. Then c
points: First rule out a pipeline bug: schema, nulls, feature code, train-serve skew
Compare feature and target distributions between 2023 and 2024
Slice performance by segment and month to find where it broke
A changed world means covariate or concept shift
Retraining helps only if the new regime is in the data
Otherwise add macro features, shorten the window or add guardrails, chosen by backtest

key_points.base: I'd diagnose before acting. If training and validation error are both high and close, that's bias: u
points: Diagnose before acting by comparing training and validation error
Both errors high and close means bias: richer model, better features, less regularization
Low training and much higher validation error means variance
Fix variance with more data, stronger regularization, a simpler model or bagging
Learning curves show which regime you are in
Regularization trades a little bias for a larger cut in variance

key_points.base: A model that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate, so accuracy tells me nothing. I'd look at pr
points: Always predicting not-fraud is 99.9% accurate, so accuracy says nothing
Use precision-recall curves and PR-AUC rather than ROC-AUC
Set the threshold from the cost of missed fraud, false alerts and review capacity
Evaluate on mature cohorts because fraud labels arrive late
Unlabeled fraud makes recall look better than it is

key_points.base: Random folds mix future and past, so the model can learn patterns from after the test period and the
points: Random k-fold mixes future into training, so scores are too optimistic
Use walk-forward validation: train up to a cutoff, test on the next period
Leave a gap between train and test when the label looks ahead
Expanding windows suit stable relationships; sliding windows adapt to drift
Tune hyperparameters inside the training period with time-aware splits

key_points.base: Not automatically. First I'd check the difference is real with a confidence interval from bootstrapp
points: Don't ship automatically on a 1% AUC gain
Check the gain is real with a confidence interval from bootstrap or repeated folds
Translate the gain into the business metric and weigh it against costs
Consider explainability, latency, fragility to drift and maintenance burden
If the gain is small, ship logistic regression or add SHAP and monitoring

key_points.base: I'd start by understanding why values are missing. If missingness is random, simple imputation is fi
points: First understand why values are missing
If missingness depends on the value, mean imputation biases; add a missing indicator
Fit imputation inside the pipeline on training data only to avoid leakage
Tree models like XGBoost handle missing values natively
Check whether outliers are errors or real extremes
Keep real outliers with robust methods or log transforms; remove only confirmed errors

key_points.base: That gap suggests the model has memorized training patterns that don't generalize, meaning high vari
points: A large train-validation gap means overfitting, high variance
First confirm the split is valid: no duplicates, similar distributions, no leakage
Use learning curves to see whether more data would help
Try a simpler model or stronger regularization and early stopping
Also feature pruning, more or augmented data, and cross-validation
Judge each change on the gap and the validation score together

key_points.base: Bagging, as in a random forest, trains many deep, high-variance trees independently on bootstrap sam
points: Bagging trains deep trees independently on bootstrap samples and averages them
Averaging cancels variance, so random forest trees can be deep
Boosting builds trees sequentially, each fitting the remaining errors, reducing bias
Boosting trees are shallow and scaled by a learning rate
Boosting is usually more accurate but more sensitive to noisy labels and tuning
A random forest is a robust low-tuning baseline

key_points.base: It depends on how the score is used. If we only rank cases and take the top K, AUC is what matters.
points: It depends on whether scores are used for ranking or as probabilities
For top-K ranking, AUC is what matters
For expected loss, pricing or cost thresholds, miscalibration causes wrong decisions
Check with a reliability diagram and the Brier score
Recalibrate on held-out data with Platt scaling or isotonic regression
Monitor calibration because it drifts when class balance shifts

key_points.base: One-hot would create 50,000 sparse columns, slow training and overfit rare values. Options: frequenc
points: One-hot encoding 50,000 values is sparse, slow and overfits rare values
Use frequency or count encoding
Target encoding must be out of fold and smoothed toward the global mean
Other options: embeddings, hashing, grouping rare values or a coarser hierarchy
CatBoost and LightGBM handle categories natively
Plan for unseen values at serving and validate with a time-based split

key_points.base: For prediction, mostly no: a regularized linear model and a boosted model predict about as well. In
points: For prediction, correlated features mostly don't matter
In a linear model, coefficients become unstable and individual signs can't be trusted
Ridge regularization or dropping one feature stabilizes a linear model
In trees, importance gets split between the two or flips between runs
For explanation, report correlated features as a group or remove one
Drop a feature for interpretation, cost or stability, not as a reflex

key_points.base: I'd turn it into expected value: flagging a customer costs the discount, and pays off only if the cu
points: Frame the threshold as expected value: discount cost versus value of a saved customer
You need the discount's real effect on churn, ideally from an experiment
High churn probability doesn't mean the customer is persuadable
Sweep thresholds on held-out data with calibrated probabilities to maximize profit
Respect capacity limits like how many offers the team can send
0.5 and F1 are arbitrary; re-tune when base rates or costs shift

key_points.base: Fanning residuals mean the error variance rises with the predicted value, known as heteroscedasticit
points: Fanning residuals mean heteroscedasticity: error variance grows with the prediction
Point predictions can stay unbiased but standard errors and intervals are wrong
Plot residuals against fitted values and each feature
Fix by modeling the log of the target or weighted least squares
Use robust standard errors or model the spread, for example quantile regression
Check the metric reflects relative error if large values matter

key_points.base: Not yet. With 400 examples a single cross-validation estimate is very uncertain, so I'd report an in
points: Don't trust it yet: a CV estimate on 400 examples is very uncertain
Report an interval and use repeated or stratified CV
Look for duplicates or the same entity split across folds
Look for a feature that encodes the label or tuning on the same folds
Use grouped splits, nested CV and an untouched holdout
Compare with a trivial baseline and check whether real data resembles the sample

key_points.base: ARIMA combines autoregression on past values (p), differencing to remove trend (d) and a moving aver
points: ARIMA combines autoregression (p), differencing (d) and a moving average of errors (q)
Differencing makes the series stationary so coefficients stay stable
Choose orders with autocorrelation plots and information criteria
Validate with walk-forward backtests
Good for a single short regular series with few drivers, and easy to explain
Poor for many series, multiple seasonalities, holidays or rich external features

key_points.base: Exponential smoothing is a quick, robust baseline for each series and needs little tuning. Prophet a
points: Exponential smoothing is a quick robust baseline per series
Prophet adds trend changes, seasonality and holidays but isn't always most accurate
Gradient boosting trains one global model across all products
A global model uses lag, calendar, price and promotion features and helps short histories
Compare all three with walk-forward validation on the business metric
Ship the simple baseline first and switch only if the global model clearly wins

key_points.base: Separate models at each level won't sum. Bottom-up sums store forecasts, which is consistent but noi
points: Separate models at each level won't add up
Bottom-up is consistent but noisy for sparse stores
Top-down is smooth but loses store detail
Reconciliation adjusts all levels jointly, weighted by reliability
Reconciliation often improves accuracy at every level
Evaluate at every level and choose by where decisions are made

key_points.base: MAPE is easy to read but explodes when actuals are near zero and penalizes over-forecasts more than
points: MAPE explodes near zero and penalizes over-forecasts more, pushing toward under-forecasting
RMSE punishes large misses, for when big misses are disproportionately costly
WAPE divides total absolute error by total actuals and weights high-volume items
Choose the metric from the cost of errors
Report more than one metric at the level where decisions are made

key_points.base: Matrix factorization learns a vector for each user and item from the interaction matrix so that thei
points: Matrix factorization learns user and item vectors from interactions
It captures taste without item attributes but struggles with new items
Content-based scores items by attribute or embedding similarity and handles new items
Content-based tends to recommend more of the same
Use implicit feedback and combine approaches, often with a ranking model on top
Evaluate offline with recall at k or NDCG on time splits, then an online experiment

key_points.base: Models based on distances (k-NN, k-means, SVMs), penalized models (ridge, lasso) and gradient-based
points: Distance-based models like k-NN, k-means and SVM need scaling
Penalized models and gradient-based models like neural networks need scaling
Tree models split on thresholds, so scaling changes nothing
Fit the scaler on training data only to avoid leakage
Standardize by default; min-max for bounded inputs; robust scaler for outliers
